extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Tatler — educated London readers and aspiring writers interested in manners, conversation, and literary composition
extracted.subtask_short: writing essays on manners and tragedy
extracted.subtask_description: Periodical-essay guidance on social conduct, conversation, and writing (especially tragic poetry/drama) — norms for comportment, rhetorical clarity, and authentic expression. Mixes moral prescription with practical examples and anecdotes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural companion in conversation
rubrics_metrics.description: The natural, and not the acquired man, is the companion. Learning, wit, gallantry, and good breeding, are all but subordinate qualities in society, and are of no value, but as they are subservient to benevolence, and tend to a certain manner of being or appearing equal to the rest of the company.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conversation should be composed of men as they are, not as distinguished by fortune; avoid emulation to excel companions; mutual goodwill is the essence of just conversation. Examples/anti-patterns: people who put on affected gravity or gaiety (‘monsters of conversation’) spoil company; bringing social quality/status into conversation is improper (see also: 'he that brings his quality with him into conversation, should always pay the reckoning').

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid displaying superiority or rank in company
rubrics_metrics.description: He that brings his quality with him into conversation, should always pay the reckoning; for he came to receive homage, and not to meet his friends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use conversation as a stage for status-seeking or to demand homage; social accomplishments (learning, wit, breeding) are valuable only insofar as they promote equality and benevolence in company. Anti-pattern: treating conversation as an opportunity to display rank or demand deference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle fops and coxcombs with ridicule or tolerant reception, not harsh contempt
rubrics_metrics.description: It will be much more easy therefore to laugh him into reason, than convert him from his foppery by any serious contempt... They are never mortified, but when they see you receive, and despise them; otherwise they rest assured, that it is your ignorance makes them out of your good graces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommended tactics for responding to vain, intrusive people: use gentle ridicule or tolerant reception to deflate their pretensions rather than stern rebuke. Examples: Sir Taffety Trippet — laughing at him, receiving him, or ignoring him may be more effective than open contempt. Warning: bitter dissuasion by friends may perversely help a fortune-hunter succeed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge by substance, not outward appearance
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not be deceived by ostentation: outward dress or airs may attract attention, but do not indicate true worth — judge a man by his actions and substance rather than feathers and high heels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by Verisimilis and the plain gentleman: the finely dressed man drew gazes but was mocked as a fop; the plain man behaved with natural confidence. Anti-pattern: assuming that fine dress equals merit; be wary of social deceit in Exchange Alley and similar contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of meaning — do not write without expressing your purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: To write without discovering your meaning, bears a just resemblance to marching without beat of drum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writings (especially poems or addresses) should clearly express their meaning; obscure or purposeless composition is criticized. Practical stylistic note: a postscript can be used to supply material forgotten in the main text — 'a postscript seems to me the more just way of apology; because otherwise a man makes an excuse before the offence is committed.' Example: the 'Brussels Postscript' poem as an instance of apt postscript use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity in tragedy: show, don't merely describe
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the common fault of those who write in the buskin style, that you give us rather the sentiments of such who behold tragical events, than of such who bear a part in them themselves... You must go to the very bottom of the heart, or it is all mere language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good tragic writing requires genuine feeling and inward knowledge of sorrow; avoid mere description or theatrical sentimentality. Read Shakespeare as a corrective: his scenes (example from 2 Henry IV) show grief by action and utterance rather than by overwrought description. Anti-pattern: producing maudlin or 'pretended' sorrow that exposes the writer's lack of authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose advisors who have lived the affliction they counsel on
rubrics_metrics.description: You are not to choose your physician for his knowledge in your distemper, but for having it himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When seeking counsel (medical, poetic, or moral), prefer those who have direct experience of the condition. Anecdote: Tom Spindle's 'spleen' cured by a poet who understood poetic vapours; Dr. Drachm's prescriptions failed where experiential remedies (poetry) succeeded. Practical implication: experiential expertise can be more effective than abstract knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of postscript as an appropriate rhetorical device
rubrics_metrics.description: A postscript is the nature of a postscript to contain something very material which was forgotten, or not clearly expressed in the letter itself... a postscript seems to me the more just way of apology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If important matter is omitted or unclear in the main text, a postscript can be a more fitting corrective than a preface or an anticipatory excuse. Example: the 'Brussels Postscript' poem was titled so because it figuratively 'wants a postscript' — i.e., it supplies what the main piece left out. Anti-pattern: burying essential meaning in oblique allusions rather than clear supplementary notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid empty labour and pretence in artistic endeavour
rubrics_metrics.description: Men of sense are professed enemies to all such empty labours: for he who pretends to be sorrowful, and is not, is a wretch yet more contemptible than he who pretends to be merry, and is not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artistic efforts should be rooted in genuine understanding and feeling; mere technical or surface knowledge (like a physician who knows disease names but not causes) does not make the practitioner/artist competent. Anti-patterns: producing works that simulate depth without possessing it; favor sincerity and inward truth.
